title: What is a commodity?
subtitle: Standardized goods - the cost driver of the entire economy
openingQuestion: Which commodity has the most direct impact on an airline's costs?
explanation: Jet fuel (from crude oil) makes up 20-30% of an airline's operating costs - the largest share of its cost structure, higher than personnel costs at many carriers. Because oil is a globally traded commodity, an airline has no pricing power over this input and has to actively hedge the risk with futures contracts.

realWorldExample.description: Uses oil futures to lock in jet fuel prices 6-12 months ahead.

quiz.question: How does a commodity differ from an ordinary product?
options: It always has a more stable price than ordinary consumer products
It's standardized so units can be substituted for each other when traded
It can only be traded domestically, never exported
The seller sets the price freely because the product is highly distinctive
quiz.explanation: Because it's standardized and traded on global exchanges (like CME, ICE), a commodity's price is set by worldwide supply and demand, leaving individual sellers/buyers almost no ability to influence the price - this is the 'price taker' trait.

quiz.question: When crude oil prices rise sharply, which group of businesses is usually hit HARDEST on cost?
options: Commercial banks and life insurance companies
Domestic essential-goods retailers
Airlines, transportation, and manufacturers that use a lot of fuel
Domestic oil and gas exploration and refining companies
quiz.explanation: A rising commodity price is a double-edged sword: it benefits producers/extractors of that commodity, but it's a cost burden for industries using it as a main input, like aviation (fuel), transportation, or manufacturing (raw materials).

quiz.question: Why do airlines like Vietnam Airlines often use futures contracts to 'lock in' fuel prices 6-12 months ahead?
options: To buy fuel at a price below the market rate
Because aviation law requires locking in prices 6 months ahead
To speculate for profit from future oil price differences
To hedge against the risk of fuel price volatility
quiz.explanation: Hedging with futures lets a business with a large input cost (like flight fuel making up 20-30% of operating costs) actively manage price-volatility risk, instead of leaving profit entirely dependent on the unpredictable movements of the commodity market.

quiz.question: An airline locks in fuel prices with a futures contract, then the oil price falls sharply. What happens?
options: They still have to buy at the locked-in price, missing out on the benefit of the price drop
They get to buy at the new market price because the contract cancels itself when prices fall
They earn a large gain on the contract since hedging always benefits from market volatility
They only pay the price difference and get the entire fee refunded
quiz.explanation: Hedging buys certainty, not profit: it cuts off both the bad tail and the good tail. In exchange, the airline can plan ticket prices and costs for the whole year - worth more to an industry where fuel makes up most of its operating costs.

quiz.question: Why can't a commodity-extracting business usually raise its selling price when its production costs rise?
options: Because antitrust law bans businesses in this industry from adjusting their selling price
Because the product is nearly identical, so global supply and demand set the price
Because commodity sales contracts are always signed at a permanently fixed price
Because their production costs never change meaningfully from year to year
quiz.explanation: A barrel of the same grade oil is identical no matter who sells it, so the buyer only looks at price. Businesses in this industry are price takers: their profit depends on how low their extraction cost is, not on any pricing power.

keyTakeaways: Spot vs Futures: contango vs backwardation
Analysis: who benefits, who's hurt when a commodity's price rises?

practicePrompt.question: Binh manages a small airline and sees crude oil prices swinging hard, unsure whether they'll rise or fall next year. Why should he consider using futures contracts to lock in fuel prices ahead of time, instead of just buying at the spot price whenever he needs it?
options: To hedge against fuel price volatility, fixing his largest input cost in advance
To speculate for extra profit from the oil price spread, since that's the main purpose of fuel futures contracts
Because international aviation law requires every airline to use futures contracts to buy fuel
Because the futures price is always lower than the spot price, so futures always save money in every case
practicePrompt.explanation: Hedging with futures fixes the fuel cost - the airline's largest input cost - in advance, to make profit more predictable, not to speculate for gains from price swings.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Spot vs Futures: contango vs backwardation

application.title: Look it up now
application.message: The lesson gave a real example of fuel costs at Vietnam Airlines - review the 'A real example' section above. Now look up a different transportation company yourself and apply that same reading approach.
application.secondary: This is the most intuitive way to see how a commodity affects a business's profit.

sections.text: From your morning cup of coffee to the plane ticket you buy, the price of nearly everything in the economy is influenced by a group of raw goods called commodities - crude oil, metals, agricultural products. Understanding commodities means understanding one of the most important 'cost drivers' shaping business profit worldwide.

A commodity is a product standardized in quality and specification to the point that one unit from one supplier can fully substitute for a unit from another - a barrel of WTI crude oil in Texas trades essentially identically to a barrel of WTI elsewhere. This exact standardization is what lets commodities trade on global exchanges (CME, ICE, LME) at a single price set by worldwide supply and demand.
Price taker: the core trait of a commodity market

Because the good is standardized and traded globally, an individual producer or buyer has almost no pricing power - they're a 'price taker', unlike many other industries where a business can set prices based on brand, differentiated quality, or its own production cost. An oil-extraction company in Vietnam can't sell crude oil at a price higher than the world market rate just because its extraction cost is higher - it has to sell at the going rate, whether it's profitable or not.

items: Crude oil: directly affects transportation, aviation, plastics, and chemical costs
Industrial metals (copper, aluminum, steel): affect construction, electronics manufacturing, and automotive costs
Agricultural products (corn, soybeans, coffee, rice): affect food, livestock, and beverage costs
Precious metals (gold, silver): usually seen more as a safe-haven asset than a production input

sections.text: Spot and Futures: two ways to trade a commodity

The 'spot' price is the price for immediate purchase and delivery. The 'futures' price is a price agreed today for delivery at a specific future date. When the futures price is higher than the spot price, the market is in 'contango' (usually reflecting expectations of rising prices, or storage/financing costs); when the futures price is lower than the spot price, it's called 'backwardation' (usually happening when current supply is scarce).

sections.label: Why a business should care about a commodity even without trading it directly
sections.text: When analyzing a business for investment, an investor needs to clearly identify which commodity is that business's main 'cost driver', and how a rise or fall in that commodity's price would affect its profit margin. For example, rising oil prices are bad news for an airline but can be good news for an oil and gas exploration company - the exact same commodity price move has completely opposite effects depending on the business's position in the value chain.
A real example: fuel costs at Vietnam Airlines

items: Jet fuel (Jet A1) makes up about 30-40% of Vietnam Airlines' total operating costs - the largest share of the airline's cost structure
Every 1 USD/barrel rise in fuel price above plan adds more than 300 billion VND/year to the airline's costs - illustrating high sensitivity to commodity prices
This is why airline stocks often swing hard with world oil prices, even though the company itself doesn't directly "trade oil"

sections.label: How to look this up yourself for another company
sections.text: Open the financial statements (the notes on cost of goods sold/selling expenses) of a transportation or airline company on the company's IR page or Vietstock, and find the "fuel cost" line to see the actual proportion.

lines: Commodities are the hidden cost foundation behind almost every industry in the economy - understanding who benefits and who loses when commodity prices move is an important analytical skill.
When assessing a business, always ask: which commodity does this business depend on as an input or output, and what tools (like futures contracts) does it have to manage that price-volatility risk?
